templates.pattern: A Carnot heat engine operates between a hot reservoir at [TH] K and a cold reservoir at [TC] K. Calculate the maximum theoretical efficiency of the engine as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Carnot efficiency = (1 − Tc ÷ Th) × 100
= ((Th − Tc) ÷ Th) × 100
= (([TH] − [TC]) ÷ [TH]) × 100
= [TH-TC] ÷ [TH] × 100
= [RESULT]%

The Carnot engine gives the maximum possible efficiency between two temperatures. No real engine can exceed this value.

templates.pattern: A transformer has [N1] turns on the primary coil and [N2] turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is [V1] V. Calculate the secondary voltage in volts.
templates.explanation:
Transformer equation: V2 ÷ V1 = N2 ÷ N1
V2 = V1 × N2 ÷ N1
= [V1] × [N2] ÷ [N1]
= [RESULT] V

A step-up transformer has more secondary turns and increases voltage. A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns and decreases voltage.

templates.pattern: A transformer has [N1] turns on the primary coil and [N2] turns on the secondary coil. The primary current is [I1] A. Calculate the secondary current in amperes. (Assume 100% efficiency)
templates.explanation:
For an ideal transformer: V1I1 = V2I2
Combining with V2/V1 = N2/N1:
I2 = I1 × N1 ÷ N2
= [I1] × [N1] ÷ [N2]
= [RESULT] A

When a transformer steps up voltage it steps down current proportionally to conserve power.

templates.pattern: A power transmission line has a resistance of [R] Ω and carries a current of [I] A. Calculate the power wasted as heat in the transmission line in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power lost = I² × R
= [I]² × [R]
= [I*I] × [R]
= [RESULT] W

This is why electricity is transmitted at very high voltages — higher voltage means lower current for the same power, which dramatically reduces transmission losses.

templates.pattern: A solar panel of area [A] m² receives solar irradiance of [G] W/m² and has an efficiency of [EFF]%. Calculate the electrical power output of the panel in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power output = Area × Irradiance × Efficiency
= [A] × [G] × ([EFF] ÷ 100)
= [A] × [G] × [EFF/100]
= [RESULT] W

Typical solar panel efficiencies are between 15% and 22%. The remaining energy is reflected or converted to heat.

templates.pattern: A system has three components with efficiencies of [E1]%, [E2]% and [E3]%. Calculate the overall efficiency of the complete system as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Overall efficiency = (E1 ÷ 100) × (E2 ÷ 100) × (E3 ÷ 100) × 100
= E1 × E2 × E3 ÷ 10000
= [E1] × [E2] × [E3] ÷ 10000
= [RESULT]%

Efficiencies in a chain multiply together. Even three components each 80% efficient give an overall efficiency of only 51.2%.

templates.pattern: An object of mass [M] kg is launched vertically upward at [V] m/s. Calculate the maximum height reached by the object in metres. (g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance)
templates.explanation:
Using conservation of energy: KE = GPE at maximum height
½mv² = mgh
h = v² ÷ 2g
= [V]² ÷ (2 × 10)
= [V*V] ÷ 20
= [RESULT] m

Mass cancels out — the maximum height does not depend on the mass of the object.

templates.pattern: A fuel has an energy density of [ED] MJ/kg. A [M] kg sample is burned with [EFF]% efficiency. Calculate the useful energy released in megajoules.
templates.explanation:
Useful energy = energy density × mass × efficiency
= [ED] × [M] × ([EFF] ÷ 100)
= [ED] × [M] × [EFF/100]
= [RESULT] MJ

No combustion process is 100% efficient. Some energy is always lost as heat to the surroundings.

templates.pattern: A power station has a useful power output of [PO] MW and a total power input of [PI] MW. Calculate the efficiency of the power station as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Efficiency = (Useful Power Output ÷ Total Power Input) × 100
= ([PO] ÷ [PI]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

Most thermal power stations have efficiencies between 30% and 45%. Combined cycle gas turbines can reach 60%.

templates.pattern: A wind turbine has blades sweeping an area of [A] m². The wind speed is [V] m/s and the air density is 1.2 kg/m³. Calculate the maximum power available from the wind in watts.
templates.explanation:
Wind power = ½ × air density × swept area × wind speed³
= 0.5 × 1.2 × [A] × [V]³
= 0.6 × [A] × [V*V*V]
= [RESULT] W

Wind power depends on the cube of wind speed — doubling wind speed increases available power eightfold. Real turbines extract around 40% of this theoretical maximum.
